tier_reason: eBACS/eBASH is a well-known independent suite. SUPERCOP is public, and the alder test-results page gives the compiler and flags for every implementation, so the method would reach A for the algorithm. The headline LSH numbers come from SUPERCOP's own avx2 (LSH-512) and ssse3 (LSH-256) implementations, not from the cataloged Crypto++ code, so the tier stays at B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: eBASH amd64-alder (Core i3-12100), long-message medians: LSH-512 2.14 cycles/byte vs BLAKE2b 3.36 (~1.57x) and SHA3-512 11.25 (~5.26x); LSH-256 3.13 vs BLAKE2s 5.24 (~1.67x) and SHA3-256 5.96 (~1.90x) (ratios derived from page data). Both variants also win at 576-4096 bytes but lose at 64 bytes (LSH-512 9.52, LSH-256 7.27 vs BLAKE2b 7.04, BLAKE2s 4.84 cycles/byte). BLAKE3 (1.73) and SHA-256 (2.05) are faster than both LSH variants on long messages. SUPERCOP's Crypto++-derived 'cryptopp' implementation is 2.92x slower than the best LSH-512 (11240 vs 3854 in the test-results Time column), which is ~2.2x slower than BLAKE2b's best (5142) but still ~1.56x faster than SHA3-512 (17498). For LSH-256 it is only 1.05x slower than the best (5503), still ~1.46x faster than BLAKE2s (8016) and ~1.74x faster than SHA3-256 (9597) (derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: BLAKE2 (BLAKE2b vs LSH-512, BLAKE2s vs LSH-256) and SHA-3 (SHA3-512 / SHA3-256). Each eBASH row is the fastest SUPERCOP implementation of that function. For SHA-3 the winner is 'oncore64bits'; OpenSSL's SHA-3 is also measured and is 1.27-1.28x slower.
corrections.workload: eBASH/SUPERCOP crypto_hash timings on amd64-alder. Long-message cycles/byte is 1/16384 of the cycle-count difference between hashing 18208-byte and 1824-byte messages (per the page). Rows are medians (StQ2) of many measurements. The page also lists 8/64/576/1536/4096-byte figures.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Per implementation on alder (SUPERCOP keeps the fastest compiler/flag combination; all use -fwrapv -fPIC -fPIE). LSH-512 avx2: Debian Clang 19.1.7 -march=native -O2. LSH-256 ssse3: Clang 19.1.7 -march=native -Os. BLAKE2b regs: gcc 14.2.0 -march=native -mtune=native -O. BLAKE2s avxicc: Clang 19.1.7 -march=native -O. SHA3-512 oncore64bits: gcc 14.2.0 -march=native -mtune=native -O2. SHA3-256 oncore64bits: gcc 14.2.0 -O3. Crypto++-derived LSH-512: g++ -march=native -mtune=native -O. Crypto++-derived LSH-256: clang++ -march=native -O3.
corrections.license: BSL-1.0 (the Crypto++ compilation is under the Boost Software License 1.0; individual files, including lsh256*/lsh512*.cpp, are placed in the public domain)
corrections.caveats: The eBASH headline numbers come from SUPERCOP's own avx2 (LSH-512) and ssse3 (LSH-256) implementations, not from Crypto++. SUPERCOP also benchmarks a 'cryptopp' LSH implementation: on alder it is 2.92x slower than the best for LSH-512, which puts it behind BLAKE2b, and 1.05x slower for LSH-256. It is not known whether that build uses Crypto++'s lsh512_avx.cpp path. Crypto++'s LSH code (lsh256/lsh512 .cpp plus _sse/_avx) was written by Jeffrey Walton from KISA's specification and reference code. LSH loses to BLAKE2 on short (64-byte and 8-byte) messages, and BLAKE3 and SHA-NI SHA-256 beat it on long messages on this CPU. IACR eprint 2015/494 (withdrawn) described free-start collision and pseudo-preimage attacks on full-round LSH, possible because LSH has no feed-forward, plus 14-round boomerang attacks; none is a practical collision on the standard hash. The ISO/IEC 10118-3 inclusion claim was not verified. The Crypto++ compilation is BSL-1.0 and the individual files are public domain.

notes: The numbers for both variants match the alder results page exactly. The compiler and flags per implementation are on https://bench.cr.yp.to/web-impl/amd64-alder-crypto_hash.html. repo_url (Crypto++) is not the code that produced the headline numbers. Consider pointing the entry at SUPERCOP's avx2/ssse3 LSH implementations; if the entry is kept as algorithm-level, A-level methodology exists. GitHub reports license NOASSERTION; License.txt says Boost 1.0 for the compilation. last_commit 2026-09-23 and active status confirmed.

tier_reason: results/64/README.md shows XXH3-64 timed in the same SMHasher3 binaries. The benchmark code is public (smhasher3/chainhash.cpp, results/64/bench/chainhash.cpp, run_speed.py, build_m2.py). CPUs are stated (Xeon Platinum 8375C, M2 Pro), as are the compilers (GCC 11.5, Apple Clang 17) and flags (M2: -O3 -march=native+crypto -DNDEBUG in build_m2.py; Xeon: SMHasher3 CMake Release, x86 paths dispatched at runtime).

corrections.claimed_speedup: SMHasher3 Speed at 262,144 bytes: 28.31 B/TSC vs XXH3-64's 19.90 on Xeon 8375C (~1.42x), and 26.26 vs 13.04 B/cycle on Apple M2 Pro (~2.01x) (ratios derived from page data). On short 1-31-byte inputs ChainHash is much slower: 155.14 vs 29.44 cycles/hash on Xeon and 87.49 vs 25.05 on M2.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Xeon: GCC 11.5, SMHasher3 CMake Release build with no global ISA flags (PCLMUL/VPCLMULQDQ/AVX-512 paths chosen at runtime), pinned to CPUs 16-23 with taskset. M2 Pro: Apple Clang 17, -O3 -march=native+crypto -std=c++11 -DNDEBUG (results/64/bench/build_m2.py). SMHasher3 --test=Speed.
corrections.caveats: The author also wrote and ran the benchmark. Raw logs, SHA-256 provenance and the bench scripts are published, but the scripts depend on a separately configured SMHasher3 checkout and are 'archived evidence rather than a runnable distribution'. The Xeon bulk figure is the higher of two passes; M2 figures are medians of three. ChainHash is bulk-only and makes no small-key speed claim: it is ~5x (Xeon) and ~3.5x (M2) slower than XXH3 on 1-31-byte inputs. The repo was created 2026-09-18 and has no independent confirmation yet.

notes: Numbers match the page exactly, and the repo checks out: MIT, 7 stars, last commit 2026-09-23, not a fork. The added caveat on short-input slowness matters for any reader thinking of it as a general XXH3 replacement.

tier_reason: The README 'Speed: Hash Short Inputs with 64-bit Seed' table compares CircleHash64f against XXH3, with Go version and CPU stated. No benchmark code is published (circlehash64_test.go has only Test functions, no Benchmark*), and the XXH3 implementation is not named, so these are first-party numbers without methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 1.05x-1.83x faster than XXH3 on 4-256-byte inputs with a 64-bit seed: 1.34 vs 1.21 GB/s at 4 B, 5.48 vs 5.21 at 16 B (smallest gain), 10.3 vs 9.33 at 64 B, 15.0 vs 8.19 GB/s at 256 B (ratios derived from page data)
corrections.hardware: darwin_amd64, Intel Core i7-1068NG7 (the README footnote writes 'i7-1068N7'; the repo description says i7-1068NG7)
corrections.caveats: No Benchmark function exists in the repo (circlehash64_test.go has correctness tests only), so the README table cannot be reproduced from published code. It is a single machine and apparently a single run. The XXH3 implementation is not named; since the benchmark ran under Go 1.17.7 it is probably a Go port, but that is unconfirmed. The author notes CircleHash64 targets inputs <= 512 bytes and gives no numbers above 256 bytes.

notes: The numbers match the README, but at 16 bytes the gain is only 1.05x, so the low end was rounded up. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 24 stars, last commit 2026-08-16, active, not a fork. This is a Go library; the XXH3 implementation used as the baseline is unnamed (probably a Go port, unconfirmed).
